Overview of the Exchange

During a recent episode of the HBO series *Real Time with Bill Maher*, host Bill Maher engaged in a tense on-air debate with guest Kid Rock. The conversation shifted from a discussion regarding a previous meeting at the White House to political rhetoric surrounding Democratic candidates, specifically Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

The Comparison to 9/11 Hijackers

During the segment, Maher questioned Kid Rock regarding comments made by former President Donald Trump about El-Sayed, who is Muslim. When asked if he believed that electing Muslim candidates would lead to an increase in Islamic extremism, Kid Rock made a controversial comparison between El-Sayed and the individuals responsible for the September 11 terrorist attacks.

  • Kid Rock's Claim: Kid Rock argued that despite El-Sayed being well-educated and appearing assimilated, historical examples of extremists had also assimilated into society before carrying out attacks.
  • The Specific Analogy: Kid Rock suggested that the 9/11 hijackers were examples of individuals who had successfully assimilated, questioning whether the candidate was a "wolf in sheep’s clothing."

Fact-Checking the Claims

Maher challenged the historical accuracy of the guest’s assertion, specifically noting that the 9/11 hijackers did not have a history of successful assimilation into American culture.

  • Verified Facts: Official reports confirm that 15 of the 19 hijackers involved in the September 11 attacks were from Saudi Arabia, with the others hailing from the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, and Lebanon.
  • Timeline: Most of these individuals entered the United States in the year 2000, contradicting the suggestion that they were long-term, assimilated residents.

How to Verify

Viewers can verify the context of this exchange by accessing the official *Real Time with Bill Maher* broadcast archives or reviewing official transcripts provided by the network. The details regarding the origins and background of the 9/11 hijackers are documented in the 9/11 Commission Report, which is publicly available through the National Archives.
